units.title: Hello, Racket
units.summary: Write your first Racket program and print text with displayln, display and printf.

lesson.md: Every Racket program starts with the line `#lang racket`. It tells Racket which language the file is written in. After it comes your code. This program prints one line of text.

`(displayln "Hello, Racket!")` is a **function call**. You write an opening parenthesis `(`, the name of the function, its arguments and a closing parenthesis `)`. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Racket!"`, is a **string**. `displayln` prints its argument and then starts a new line.
`display` prints its argument but does not start a new line. `newline` takes no arguments and only starts a new line. Racket runs the lines of a program from top to bottom.

`printf` prints a **format string**. Every `~a` in it is replaced by the next argument, in order. `\n` inside a string means a line break. `printf` does not add a line break by itself, so you usually end the format string with `\n`.
`~s` also inserts the next argument, but writes it the way it looks in code. A string then keeps its double quotes. `~a` shows only the text.

A semicolon `;` starts a **comment**: Racket ignores everything after it until the end of the line, for example `(displayln 42) ; 42`. In the exercises, the first line `#lang racket` is often left out to keep the code short.

card: `#lang racket` is the first line of every program
`(display "Hi")` prints without a line break, `(newline)` adds one
`(printf "~a and ~s\n" x y)`: `~a` as text, `~s` as code
`; comment` until the end of the line

exercises.explain: `display` does not start a new line, so both strings end up on the same line. `newline` ends it.

units.title: Values
units.summary: Calculate with numbers and exact fractions, and meet strings, symbols, booleans and define.

lesson.md: In Racket, the operator comes **first**, inside parentheses: `(+ 2 3)` means 2 plus 3. This is called **prefix notation**. The operators are `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide). `+` and `*` accept any number of arguments. You can also put a calculation inside another one: in `(* 2 (+ 3 4))`, Racket first computes `(+ 3 4)`, which is `7`, and then `(* 2 7)`.

When you divide two whole numbers, Racket gives an **exact fraction**: `(/ 10 4)` is `5/2`, not `2.5`. A number with a decimal point, like `10.0`, is a decimal number, and the result is a decimal number too. `quotient` divides and drops the rest, `remainder` gives the rest.

`(define name value)` gives a value a name. After that, you can use the name instead of the value. Names may contain a dash `-`, like `total-price`. Racket programmers write names in lowercase with dashes.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define price 12)
(define items 3)
(define total-price (* price items))
(printf "Total: ~a\n" total-price)

lesson.md: A **string** is text in double quotes, and `string-length` counts its characters. A **symbol** is a name used as a value: you write a quote `'` in front of it, like `'apple`. The **booleans** are `#t` (true) and `#f` (false).

An expression that stands alone at the top level of a program, outside of any function, is also printed. Racket prints it the way it looks in code: a string with double quotes, a symbol with its quote.
The first thing after an opening parenthesis must be a function. `(2 + 3)` is an error, because `2` is not a function. Write `(+ 2 3)`, with spaces between the parts.

card: `(define price 12)` gives a value a name

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with define and lambda, call them, and use local names with let.

lesson.md: You define a function with `(define (name parameter) body)`. The **parameter** is a name for the value you pass in. The function gives back the value of its body. Racket has no `return`: the result is always the value of the last expression.
A function can have several parameters. When you call it, you pass the arguments in the same order: in `(area 3 4)`, `width` is `3` and `height` is `4`.
A function can also print something. You call it like any other function. You can use the result of one function as the argument of another one.

`(lambda (x) body)` creates a function without a name. You can call it directly, or give it a name with `define`. In fact, `(define (triple x) ...)` is a short way to write `(define triple (lambda (x) ...))`.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define triple (lambda (x) (* 3 x)))
(displayln (triple 4))
(displayln ((lambda (a b) (+ a b)) 2 3))

lesson.md: `let` creates names that exist only inside it. You write each name with its value in square brackets, all inside one more pair of parentheses: `(let ([a 1] [b 2]) body)`. Square brackets `[ ]` work like parentheses. Racket uses them to make pairs easier to read.
A function needs exactly the number of arguments it has parameters. `(square 2 3)` is an error, because `square` takes only one argument.

card: `(define (square x) (* x x))` defines a function
`(square 5)` calls it, the result is the last expression
`(lambda (x) (* 3 x))` is a function without a name

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Compare values, ask questions with predicates and choose with if, cond, when, and, or and not.

lesson.md: Comparisons give a boolean: `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=`, `>=` and `=` (equal) compare numbers. `equal?` compares any two values, for example two strings.
A function that answers a yes-or-no question is a **predicate**. By convention, its name ends with `?`. Examples: `even?`, `odd?`, `zero?`, `positive?`, `number?` and `string?`.

`(if test then else)` checks the test. If it is true, the result is the `then` part, otherwise the `else` part. Both parts are required. `if` gives back a value, so you can use it inside other expressions.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define age 20)
(displayln (if (>= age 18) "adult" "child"))
(displayln (if (> age 30) "over 30" "30 or less"))

lesson.md: Only `#f` counts as false. Every other value counts as true, even `0` and the empty string `""`. So `(if 0 "yes" "no")` gives `"yes"`.

`cond` checks several tests in order. Each **clause** is written in square brackets: a test and its result. The first clause whose test is true gives the result, and the rest is skipped. The last clause can use `else`, which matches everything.

`(when test body ...)` runs its body only if the test is true. It has no `else` part, but the body can contain several expressions. `unless` does the opposite: it runs its body only if the test is false.
`and` is true if all its parts are true. `or` is true if at least one part is true. `not` turns `#t` into `#f` and `#f` into `#t`.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define x 7)
(displayln (and (> x 0) (< x 10)))
(displayln (or (= x 1) (= x 2)))
(displayln (not (= x 7)))

units.title: Lists
units.summary: Keep many values in a list and work with list, cons, first, rest, empty?, length and append.

lesson.md: A **list** keeps values in order. `(list 1 2 3)` creates one. `displayln` shows a list in parentheses. A quote in front of parentheses also creates a list: `'(a b c)` is a list of three symbols. `println` shows a list the way you write it in code.

`first` gives the first element. `rest` gives a list of all elements except the first. `length` counts the elements. `list-ref` gives the element at a position, called the **index**. The index starts at `0`.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define fruits (list "apple" "pear" "plum"))
(displayln (first fruits))
(displayln (rest fruits))
(displayln (length fruits))
(displayln (list-ref fruits 2))

lesson.md: `cons` puts one element in front of a list. `append` joins two or more lists. Lists in Racket never change: these functions return a **new** list, and the old list stays as it was.
The **empty list** has no elements. You write it `'()` or `empty`. `empty?` checks if a list is empty. The `rest` of a list with one element is the empty list.
`reverse` turns a list around. `(sort lst <)` sorts numbers from small to large. `(range 5)` creates the list of whole numbers from `0` up to, but not including, `5`. `(range 2 6)` starts at `2`.
Do not write `(1 2 3)` without `list` or a quote. Racket would try to call `1` as a function, which is an error. Also, `first` of an empty list is an error.

units.title: Higher-order functions
units.summary: Pass functions to other functions and process lists with map, filter, foldl and lambda.

lesson.md: In Racket, functions are values. You can pass a function to another function, like a number or a string. A function that takes another function is called a **higher-order function**. `add1` is a built-in function that adds 1 to a number.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define (twice f x)
  (f (f x)))
(displayln (twice add1 5))
(displayln (twice (lambda (n) (* n 10)) 3))

lesson.md: `(map f lst)` calls the function `f` on every element of the list and gives a new list with the results. You can pass a named function or a `lambda`.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define (square x)
  (* x x))
(displayln (map square (list 1 2 3 4)))
(displayln (map (lambda (x) (* x 10)) (list 1 2 3)))
(displayln (map string-length (list "a" "bb" "ccc")))

lesson.md: `(filter pred lst)` keeps only the elements for which the predicate `pred` is true. The order stays the same.

`(foldl f start lst)` combines all elements into one value. It begins with `start`. For every element, it calls `f` with the element and the result so far, from left to right. `(foldl + 0 (list 1 2 3))` computes `(+ 3 (+ 2 (+ 1 0)))`, which is `6`.
You can combine these functions. This program keeps the even numbers, squares them and adds up the squares: 4 + 16 + 36.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define nums (list 1 2 3 4 5 6))
(define evens (filter even? nums))
(define squares (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) evens))
(displayln (foldl + 0 squares))

lesson.md: `map` also works with two lists of the same length. It then calls the function with one element from each list: `(map + (list 1 2) (list 10 20))` gives `(11 22)`.

card: `(map f lst)` calls `f` on every element
`(filter even? lst)` keeps the matching elements
`(foldl + 0 lst)` combines all elements into one value

units.title: Recursion and loops
units.summary: Repeat work with functions that call themselves, and loop over lists with for and for/list.

lesson.md: A function can call itself. This is called **recursion**. Every recursive function needs a **base case**: a case where it stops and does not call itself again. Here, the base case is `n` = 0. Each other call prints `n` and calls the function with a smaller `n`.

The **factorial** of a number is the product of all whole numbers from 1 up to it. `(factorial 3)` computes `(* 3 (factorial 2))`, which is `(* 3 (* 2 (* 1 (factorial 0))))`, which is 6. Racket whole numbers can be as big as you need.
Many list functions follow one pattern. The base case is the empty list. Otherwise, you do something with the `first` element and call the function again on the `rest`.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define (sum lst)
  (if (empty? lst)
      0
      (+ (first lst) (sum (rest lst)))))
(define (count-items lst)
  (if (empty? lst)
      0
      (+ 1 (count-items (rest lst)))))
(displayln (sum (list 1 2 3 4)))
(displayln (count-items (list "a" "b" "c")))

lesson.md: If the base case is missing or never reached, the function calls itself again and again and the program never ends. Make sure every call gets closer to the base case, for example with `(- n 1)` or `(rest lst)`.
`for` runs its body once for every element of a list. In `(for ([i (range 1 4)]) body)`, the name `i` takes each value in turn. The square brackets hold the name and the list, as in `let`.
`for` gives no useful result. `for/list` works like `for`, but collects the value of the body for every element into a new list.
`for/sum` adds up the values of the body: `(for/sum ([i (range 1 5)]) i)` gives `10`.

card: Recursion: a function calls itself on a smaller problem
Base case: `(if (empty? lst) 0 ...)` stops the recursion
`(for/list ([x lst]) (* x 2))` collects results in a list
`(for/sum ([i lst]) i)` adds up the results

units.title: Structs and strings
units.summary: Work with string functions, group values in structs and look up values by key in hashes.

lesson.md: `string-append` joins strings into one. `string-upcase` and `string-downcase` change letters to upper or lower case. `(substring s start end)` gives the characters from index `start` up to, but not including, index `end`.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define first-name "Ada")
(define last-name "Lovelace")
(displayln (string-append first-name " " last-name))
(displayln (string-upcase first-name))
(displayln (substring last-name 0 4))

lesson.md: `number->string` turns a number into a string, and `string->number` does the opposite. `string-split` splits a string at its spaces into a list of strings. `string-join` joins a list of strings with a separator between them.

A **struct** groups several values under one name. `(struct book (title pages))` defines a new kind of value with two **fields**. Racket then creates the function `book` to make a book, `book-title` and `book-pages` to read the fields, and the predicate `book?`. With `#:transparent`, `println` shows the field values.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(struct book (title pages) #:transparent)
(define b (book "Dune" 412))
(println b)
(displayln (book-title b))
(displayln (book-pages b))
(displayln (book? b))

lesson.md: Structs work well with everything you know. Here, a list of structs is passed to `map` with a field function, and `foldl` adds up the prices.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(struct item (name price))
(define cart (list (item "tea" 3) (item "cake" 5)))
(displayln (map item-name cart))
(displayln (foldl + 0 (map item-price cart)))

lesson.md: A **hash** stores pairs of a **key** and a value. `(hash "Ada" 36 "Linus" 21)` creates one. `hash-ref` looks up the value for a key, with an optional default value as third argument. `hash-set` gives a new hash with one more pair, and the old hash stays the same. `hash-count` counts the pairs, and `hash-has-key?` checks for a key.

lesson.code:
#lang racket
(define ages (hash "Ada" 36 "Linus" 21))
(displayln (hash-ref ages "Ada"))
(displayln (hash-ref ages "Bob" 0))
(define more (hash-set ages "Bob" 50))
(displayln (hash-count more))
(displayln (hash-count ages))
(displayln (hash-has-key? more "Bob"))

lesson.md: `hash-ref` with a key that does not exist and no default value is an error. A hash has no fixed order, so do not rely on the order in which its pairs are printed.
